checkpoints: A counter that accumulates a lifetime total per IP and never resets measures everything that IP has ever done, not how fast it is clicking right now — fraud detection needs a rate, not a cumulative total.

A shared office NAT or a genuinely popular ad's IP can rack up ordinary traffic over days and eventually cross a fixed lifetime threshold, producing a false positive on completely legitimate traffic with zero relation to any burst.

A lifetime counter has no concept of a burst: an IP that has been quiet for weeks and suddenly fires hundreds of clicks in seconds gets flagged no faster than one that trickles in slowly, because both are just adding to the same never-resetting number.
An ever-growing Map keyed by IP that is never cleared is also an unbounded memory leak, and once an IP is flagged it stays flagged forever with no way to cool down.

Keying counts by (IP, windowStart) instead of IP alone — for example a tumbling one-minute window compared against a per-window threshold — turns the signal into clicks-per-window rather than clicks-ever, catching a real spike the moment it happens and resetting cleanly every window.

Because the underlying signal is IP alone with a fixed constant threshold, a botnet can trivially evade it by rotating through many IPs, keeping each individual IP's count comfortably under threshold while the aggregate attack volume stays huge.

A strict tumbling window has its own boundary gap: a burst split across two adjacent windows can stay under threshold in each window even though it is really one continuous spike, so a sliding or hopping window is needed to close that gap.

A robust redesign layers signals beyond IP — device fingerprint, user agent, click-pattern behavior — and derives thresholds adaptively from each IP's own recent baseline instead of applying one hard constant to every IP on the platform.

The redesign can be validated with targeted tests: a burst of clicks from one IP within a single window must flag, the same total volume spread evenly over weeks must not flag, and a burst split across a window boundary should expose the tumbling-window gap.
